Let’s dive into Chapter 4—Generating Options for Mutual Gain: Expanding the Pie.
Now, once the real interests are out in the open, the next move is to search for ways to satisfy them. But here’s where a lot of negotiations get stuck—people tend to focus on a single solution, fiercely defending what they want. It’s that classic “fixed pie” mindset, where it seems like any gain for you is a loss for me.
But what if you could expand the pie?
Most negotiations actually have room to create more value—for both sides. The key is to be creative, open-minded, and willing to look past the obvious options.
Of course, there are some common roadblocks that can get in the way:
First, there’s premature judgment. Sometimes, we shoot down ideas too quickly because we’re worried they’ll make us look weak, or maybe just unrealistic.
Then, there’s the urge to chase after “the” answer. If you’re only searching for one perfect solution, you end up limiting your options before you even start.
Another big one? Assuming the pie is fixed—thinking there’s only so much to go around. That shuts down collaboration fast.
And finally, there’s the belief that solving their problem is their problem. If you only focus on your own needs, you’re missing out on the potential for joint gains.
So, how do you break through these barriers? It really helps to separate inventing options from deciding on them. In other words, brainstorm first—without judging or editing—then go back and evaluate later.
Here are a few practical ways to make that happen:
Start by brainstorming together. Set aside some time where both sides can throw out as many ideas as possible, with no criticism or judgment. This is your chance to be creative and see what sticks.
Next, look for shared interests. Try to find those areas where both sides stand to gain, and see if you can build solutions around them.
Don’t forget to explore your differences. Sometimes, what’s really important to one side isn’t such a big deal to the other. That opens the door for smart trade-offs that leave everyone better off.
And, of course, invent options for mutual gain. Get creative with the form, timing, or even the scope of an agreement. Is there a way to meet both sets of interests by adjusting these details?
Let’s take a real-world example. Imagine two companies working out a business partnership. One wants faster delivery, while the other is hoping for a longer contract. By adjusting the terms—say, offering a longer commitment in exchange for expedited service—both sides end up getting more of what they want.
Think of negotiation like a puzzle. The pieces can be rearranged in all sorts of ways—the goal isn’t to “win” at the other’s expense, but to find a configuration that fits everyone’s needs as well as possible.
And remember, generating options for mutual gain isn’t about being naïve or giving up too much. It’s about seeing that collaboration can create value competition just can’t match. When both sides work together to invent solutions, you usually end up with agreements that are more satisfying, more lasting, and way more likely to actually work in the real world.
